summary: Argues that the Host-IMP interface should run at the highest practical speed. A faster interface reduces delay for short messages queued behind a full-sized one, which could tie up a 100 kbps interface for nearly 100 ms.

eli5.summary: A slow road makes small cars wait behind a big truck. This note says to widen the road between the computer and the network box.

questions: why speed up the host to imp link
subtitle: Why the link between a host and its network interface processor should run as fast as possible.

tldr.problem: The Host-IMP interface running at 100 kilobaud created bottlenecks: short messages waited behind full-sized ones, buffer lock times increased, and error detection suffered.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC presents experimental results from BBN showing that both the host-to-IMP and IMP-to-host connections could operate at speeds of 290 to 310 kilobaud with simple synchronization changes, triple the existing speed.
tldr.outcome: Faster interfaces reduced message latency, improved error handling, and enabled greater bandwidth for distributed computing within and across the ARPANET.

today: RFC 594 is a historical account of early ARPANET performance optimization. The principle—that interfaces should operate at their maximum practical speed—remains valid in modern networks.

sections.title: The Bottleneck
sections.content:
In the early 1970s, host computers connected to the ARPANET through an interface to an IMP (Interface Message Processor), the network's local switching equipment. This Host-IMP interface was running at 100 kilobaud (100 kbps), creating a performance bottleneck.

A full-sized message (the maximum that could fit in one network packet) would tie up the 100 kbps interface for nearly 100 milliseconds. During that time, any small messages or protocol control signals would be queued, experiencing unacceptable delays.
sections.eli5: One big truck taking up the whole highway for 100 milliseconds meant all the small cars behind it had to wait.

sections.title: Experimental Results
sections.content:
The RFC describes an experiment by the BBN-TENEX team testing the actual hardware capabilities of host and IMP distant interfaces. The host-to-IMP connection, synchronized by a two-way handshake, achieved a burst bandwidth of 310 kilobaud. The IMP-to-host connection, which required a more complex four-way handshake, reached 290 kilobaud.

Both System A (BBN-TENEX) and System B were then operated at these higher speeds, proving feasibility. File transfer tests showed dramatic improvements: 36-bit transfers jumped from roughly 25 kbaud to around 80 kbaud.
sections.eli5: Testing showed the hardware could handle three times the traffic. When they turned it up, file transfers got three times faster.

sections.title: Benefits and Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies four main benefits of higher-speed interfaces: reduced latency for small messages; fewer buffer lock situations (where buffers are tied up during transfer); improved error detection by delaying RFNM acknowledgments until all packets are received; and greater overall bandwidth for distributed computing, especially important for network-structured sites where multiple specialized hosts share one IMP.

The authors recommend that all Host-IMP interfaces in the network be upgraded to the fastest speed obtainable.
sections.eli5: Fast lanes let short messages pass quickly, free up buffer space faster, catch transmission errors better, and let multiple computers on the same site work together.
